title: Indicator Removal
summary: Indicator removal is the deliberate editing or deletion of the records that show what an intruder did, and the defining feature in current reporting is selectivity rather than wholesale wiping. Rather than destroying a whole log, which is loud and obvious, an attacker targets the artefacts that look anomalous and leaves enough ordinary data behind that the system still appears to be behaving normally. The affected artefacts are platform specific. Command histories, shell history files, event logs, application logs, file system timestamps, file metadata, and records of scheduled tasks or services can all be trimmed, rewritten, or made to look like routine user activity. The technique does not usually prevent detection outright, but it lowers the fidelity of the alerting: a cleared log produces one clean event, while an edited log produces a timeline that no longer matches reality. Forensic value is asymmetric, which is important to understand. Data deleted from disk may be recoverable through file system analysis, and events already forwarded to a central collector are out of reach of a host based cleanup. Detection therefore relies on the shape of the data as much as its content: a gap in an otherwise continuous event sequence, a security log cleared event such as Windows Security 1102, file timestamps older than the file content or inconsistent with the directory entry, and a host that stops reporting to its log forwarder while remaining online.

beginner.definition: Computers keep records of what happens, such as commands typed and files changed. These records are called artefacts. This technique is an attacker changing or deleting some of those records. The aim is to make their actions harder to see afterwards.
beginner.whyItMatters: If the records are gone, it is hard to know what happened and what was touched. You may also struggle to prove when the intrusion began. Attackers often delete only a few entries, so the system still looks normal. That quiet approach makes the change easy to overlook.
howItWorks: The attacker first decides which records would point at their activity.
They delete or rewrite those specific entries rather than wiping everything.
Command histories, log entries and file details can all be altered this way.
They leave ordinary records in place so the system still looks healthy.
Files may be given older dates so they look like they were always there.
Copies already sent to a central log server cannot be changed from the host.
beginner.example: Imagine a factory where every visitor signs a book at the gate. A thief signs in like everyone else, does his work, then carefully tears out only his own page. The book still looks busy, and the guard sees a full day of names. Removing one page is far quieter than burning the whole book, and it raises far fewer questions. Indicator removal is that torn page.
takeaways: Send logs to a central server the host itself cannot edit.
A gap in a record is itself evidence, even when the detail is missing.
Watch for files whose dates do not match their contents.

objectives: Explain what an artefact is and why an attacker would change one.
Describe why selective editing is harder to notice than deleting a whole log.
Identify the evidence that a log or file was altered rather than simply absent.
Explain how central log collection limits the value of this technique.
Recognise routine log rotation and retention activity that can look like tampering.
